nameStory: The cinnamon fern gets its delicious name from its fertile fronds, which emerge in spring as stunning cinnamon-brown spore-bearing stalks. These rusty-colored reproductive fronds stand tall in the center of each clump, looking remarkably like cinnamon sticks rising from the forest floor. By midsummer, these brown fronds have released their spores and withered away, leaving behind the mystery of the name for those who missed the spring show.
description: Cinnamon fern is a large, showy fern that forms impressive clumps in wet areas throughout New England. It produces two distinctly different types of fronds: green sterile fronds that can reach 3-5 feet tall, and shorter cinnamon-brown fertile fronds that appear in spring. The green fronds are once-divided with oblong leaflets that taper to points, creating an elegant vase-like shape around the central brown fertile fronds. This is one of our most recognizable native ferns when the characteristic brown spore-bearing fronds are present.

idTips.label: Fertile Fronds
idTips.description: Look for the telltale cinnamon-brown fertile fronds in the center of each clump during spring and early summer - they're completely brown, lack any green leaflets, and feel papery to the touch when mature

idTips.label: Fronds
idTips.description: Green sterile fronds are once-divided with 12-20 pairs of oblong leaflets that feel smooth and have a slight sheen - each leaflet tapers to a point and attaches directly to the main stem without a stalk

idTips.label: Fiddleheads
idTips.description: Spring fiddleheads are densely covered in white to light brown woolly hairs that feel soft and fuzzy to the touch - they're much fluffier than most other fern fiddleheads

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms large, circular clumps with fronds arising from a central crown - the green fronds create a vase shape around the inner brown fertile fronds

idTips.label: Stipe
idTips.description: The stem (stipe) is thick, grooved, and covered with brown scales at the base - it makes up about one-third of the total frond length

habitat: Cinnamon ferns thrive in consistently moist to wet soils in swamps, bogs, stream banks, and moist woodlands throughout New England. You'll often find them growing alongside skunk cabbage, sensitive fern, and red maple in areas that stay damp year-round. They prefer acidic soils and partial shade, though they can tolerate full sun if the soil remains wet enough.

seasonality.spring: Woolly white fiddleheads emerge in April-May, quickly followed by the distinctive brown fertile fronds that give this fern its name. This is the best time for positive identification when both frond types are visible.
seasonality.summer: Green sterile fronds reach full size while brown fertile fronds wither and disappear by midsummer after releasing spores. The green fronds form distinctive circular clumps.
seasonality.fall: Green fronds turn golden-yellow before dying back with the first hard frost, creating beautiful autumn displays in wetland areas.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with all fronds dead - only the underground rhizome and next year's developing fiddleheads remain, protected under leaf litter and snow.

funFact: Cinnamon fern is a living fossil - virtually identical fossils of this species have been found in rocks from the Triassic period, meaning this exact same fern was growing alongside the very first dinosaurs over 200 million years ago!
confusionNotes: Royal fern is most similar with its once-divided fronds and wetland habitat, but royal fern's leaflets are more rounded and it produces brown spores at the tips of regular green fronds rather than on separate cinnamon-colored stalks. Memory trick: cinnamon fern has separate cinnamon sticks, royal fern has brown crowns on green fronds.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'cinnamon fern,' it's not related to the cinnamon spice tree at all - the name refers purely to the color of its fertile fronds. This fern was recently moved to its own genus (Osmundastrum) from the genus Osmunda based on genetic studies, so you may see it listed under either name in older field guides.
compareHints: Cinnamon fern is the only species in its genus Osmundastrum, making it unique among New England ferns. Within the royal fern family, it's easily distinguished from royal fern by its separate brown fertile fronds versus royal fern's brown spore clusters on green frond tips. Interrupted fern is similar but has brown spore-bearing sections in the middle of otherwise green fronds, not completely separate brown fronds.
